title: India’s security policy must be framed keeping in view emerging global challenges, including geopolitical instability, energy and resource insecurity, rising radicalisation and cyber misinformation campaigns, says Home Minister
author: Vijaita Singh
content_html:
Union Home Minister Amit Shah on Tuesday (August 25, 2026) said India’s security policy must be framed keeping in view emerging global challenges, including geopolitical instability, energy and resource insecurity, supply chain disruptions, rising radicalisation and cyber misinformation campaigns, while urging security agencies to anticipate threats before they become major crises.

Mr. Shah said he had visited all land-border States over the past eight months and shared with them a document outlining a four-pronged border security strategy. Stating that the government aimed to make the country “infiltrator-free” in a short period, he said illegal immigrants posed threats to national security, the economy and demographic balance. “This country is not a dharamshala and only citizens of the country have the right to live here,” he said.

Addressing the valedictory session of the Intelligence Bureau’s National Security Strategy Conference (NSSC), Mr. Shah said the forum should study trends over the next 15-20 years and identify potential security challenges and strategies to counter them. “We have to identify challenges in advance and destroy them before they become major problems,” he said, calling for the creation of an ecosystem capable of delivering a secure, infiltrator-free and narcotics-free India.

Linking national security with the government’s long-term development agenda, Mr. Shah said Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s goal of making India a developed nation by 2047 could only be achieved with strong internal security. “If we want to become number one in every field, internal security will have to be strengthened further,” he said.

The Home Minister said previous governments had failed to anticipate problems such as narcotics trafficking, Left-wing extremism and unrest in the Northeast before they became acute, forcing the country to deal with their consequences for decades. He said the government had succeeded in overcoming challenges posed by the three major internal security hotspots, crediting State police forces, Central agencies and the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPFs) for the achievement.

New criminal laws

Mr. Shah said the three new criminal laws would be implemented fully within a year. According to him, their implementation would enable criminal cases to be disposed of up to the Supreme Court level within three years and increase conviction rates by 25%.

On counter-terrorism, the Home Minister called for taking the anti-terror framework “Prahar” from a policy document to everyday practice and urged agencies to dismantle “360-degree terrorist networks”. He cited the coordinated nationwide action against the Popular Front of India (PFI) and its subsequent ban as an example of effective Centre-State coordination.

Mr. Shah also asked State police forces to implement the Narcotics Control Vision Document 2026-2029 and work on the three pillars of “Detect, Disrupt and Destroy” to achieve the goal of a drug-free India. He said the fight against narcotics could be won only through coordinated action by the Union government and all State governments.

Highlighting the role of technology in policing, Mr. Shah said integrated databases linking CCTNS, ICJS, NatGrid and NAFIS had been created. He urged young officers to use artificial intelligence for data integration, analysis and identifying criminal modus operandi to generate actionable intelligence and prevent future threats.

The Home Minister further said the government had strengthened mechanisms against fugitive offenders and that around 274 fugitives had been brought back to India from abroad between 2019 and 2026. He urged all States to work towards ensuring that offenders hiding overseas were brought within the ambit of Indian law.

title: Postpone Census to first hold tripartite talks on NRC, citizenship issues: Manipur civil society groups
author: Vijaita Singh
content_html:
A delegation of Manipur civil society organisations (CSOs) has urged the Union Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) to convene tripartite talks involving the Union government, the Manipur government, and representatives of different communities before proceeding with the Census, arguing that citizenship-related concerns must be addressed first to ensure the exercise is accepted across the State.

Leaders of a 14-member CSO platform, who have met Union Minister Kiren Rijiju, BJP president Nitin Nabin, and MHA officials in Delhi over the past few days, said they want the government to postpone Census-related activities and initiate a dialogue process on the implementation of a National Register of Citizens (NRC)-type mechanism in Manipur. While they declined to disclose details of those discussions, they said they had been assured that their concerns were being considered.

“We have requested the Government of India to organise a table where all stakeholders can sit together and discuss the issue,” delegation member Shanta Nahakpam said on Tuesday. “In the current situation, only the Centre can bring different communities together.”

Migration, citizenship concerns

The demand for tripartite talks comes amid opposition to the Census process by several Meitei organisations and a section of the Naga community in Manipur. These groups argue that carrying out the Census without first addressing concerns over illegal immigration and citizenship could affect future political representation, particularly in the context of delimitation exercises.

The delegation maintained that any citizenship verification exercise should use 1951 as the base year, arguing that the first post-Independence Census in Manipur was built on records prepared before the State’s merger with the Indian Union in 1949. According to them, pre-merger electoral rolls, village records, and population data provide the most reliable basis for identifying “original Indian citizens” in the State.

Delegation members claimed that demographic changes recorded in Census data over several decades have raised questions about population growth and the proliferation of villages in some areas. Referring to Census figures from 1961 to 2011, they alleged that while some districts recorded a decline in the number of villages, others witnessed sharp increase. Such changes warrant scrutiny, they said.

Documentary evidence needed

The organisations linked these concerns to migration from neighbouring Myanmar, citing decades of cross-border movement. They argued that after Manipur’s traditional permit system was abolished in the early years after the merger with the Indian union, there was no effective mechanism to document who entered the State and settled there.

Delegation members stressed that their demand was not directed against any particular community. Rather, they said, any future verification process should allow every resident an opportunity to establish citizenship through documentary evidence.

“This is not about targeting any tribe or community. The process should give every individual the chance to prove citizenship through records and due process,” said Ahao Kom, another member.

Census faces opposition

The groups also pointed to ongoing ethnic tensions and large-scale displacement in the State, arguing that current conditions are not conducive to a credible Census exercise. They contended that internally displaced persons, restrictions on movement between some hill and valley areas, and continuing mistrust between communities could undermine public confidence in the enumeration process.

According to the delegation, several district-level Census training programmes for enumerators have already faced opposition from local organisations who even locked up their offices and registered protests. This reflects widespread apprehension among sections of the population about conducting the exercise before resolving citizenship-related issues, they said.

The first phase of Population Census 2027, the House Listing and Housing Census (HLO), is scheduled to take place in Manipur from September 1 to 30, but training of enumerators, mostly government school teachers, has been halted amid protests by civil society groups. The self-enumeration portal, due to be launched on August 17, is also yet to become operational, with a State government official saying a decision from the MHA is awaited.

title: Two months after Shivakumar’s RRTS push, Karnataka govt. says no corridors approved
author: Darshan Devaiah B.P.
content_html:
Despite Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar seeking the Centre’s approval in June for a Regional Rapid Transit System (RRTS) connecting Bengaluru with Mysuru, Kanakapura, Tumakuru, Chickballapur, and Kolar, the Karnataka government has now clarified that no RRTS corridor connecting Bengaluru with neighbouring cities has been approved or formulated so far.

The clarification was issued in response to a question raised in the Karnataka Legislative Council on August 18. The government stated that there are currently no approved RRTS corridors connecting Bengaluru with neighbouring cities such as Mysuru, Tumakuru, Kolar, and Chickballapur.

The development comes barely two months after Mr. Shivakumar pushed for the proposed regional rapid rail network as part of efforts to improve connectivity around Bengaluru, reduce pressure on the city’s road infrastructure, and support the growth of surrounding urban centres.

On June 10, Mr. Shivakumar met Union Minister for Housing and Urban Affairs Manohar Lal Khattar in New Delhi and submitted a proposal seeking approval for RRTS connectivity between Bengaluru and surrounding towns. The proposal was part of a broader set of infrastructure requests concerning Bengaluru’s mobility needs, including metro.

Bengaluru RRTS proposal
RRTS Corridors Proposed: 5
Bengaluru–Mysuru
Bengaluru–Kanakapura
Bengaluru–Tumakuru
Bengaluru–Chikkaballapur
Bengaluru–Kolar
Proposal submitted: On June 10, 2026 to Union Minister for Housing and Urban Affairs Manohar Lal Khattar by Karnataka CM DK Shivakumar.
Current status: No RRTS corridor approved or formulated
Feasibility study: Not conducted

The proposed network was envisioned along five corridors: Bengaluru–Mysuru, Bengaluru–Kanakapura, Bengaluru–Tumakuru, Bengaluru–Chickballapur, and Bengaluru–Kolar. The proposal was modelled on the rapid regional rail network being developed in the Delhi-NCR region.

However, the latest response in the Legislative Council indicates that the proposal has not yet progressed to the stage of an approved RRTS project.

M.B. Patil, Minister of Large and Medium Scale Industries and Infrastructure Development, also said that no feasibility study has been conducted for such a system. This means that there is currently no completed feasibility report assessing the technical, financial, and operational viability of the proposed RRTS corridors.

The Legislative Council question also sought information on coordination between the Bengaluru Suburban Rail Project (BSRP) and the proposed RRTS network, as well as consultations with the National Capital Region Transport Corporation (NCRTC), which is implementing RRTS projects in the Delhi-NCR region.

In response, Mr. Patil said that no such consultation had been undertaken. “However, officials from K-RIDE, the agency implementing the Bengaluru Suburban Rail Project, visited NCRTC projects and gained an understanding of their systems and functioning,” he added.

On the possibility of integrating the suburban rail network with a future RRTS system, the government pointed out that the Bengaluru suburban rail project uses the European Train Control System (ETCS) signalling system. The Meerut–Delhi RRTS project also uses ETCS.

Mr. Patil said K-RIDE’s suburban rail network could potentially complement an RRTS system if the network is expanded in the future.

title: Buckingham Canal back in the limelight
author: T. Ramakrishnan
content_html:
The restoration of the Buckingham Canal (B’Canal) and other water courses of Chennai has yet again occupied the attention of the authorities after the Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK)-led government came to power nearly three and a half months ago. Sections of the media have reported that the State government is examining a ₹876.35-crore plan to make a 7.2-km-long stretch of the central portion of the B’Canal — from Napier Bridge over the beach road to the Adyar river over Greenways Road in R.A. Puram — navigable again, with passenger boats, floating restaurants, and cargo movement.

Originally constructed in 1806 by Basil Cochrane and privately owned and operated by him, the waterway was then called Cochrane Canal. Initially, the length of the waterway was a little less than 18 km, with the Canal cutting through strips of land and shallow backwaters from Chennai to the Ennore estuary. Subsequently, it was extended to Pulicat Lake, opening up navigation for small craft over a distance of 40 km north of Chennai. Taken over by the government in 1837, the waterway was named the East Coast Canal and extended in 1857 to Dugarajapatnam (in Tirupati district of Andhra Pradesh, around 135 km north of Chennai). In 1878, it acquired the present name, Buckingham Canal, after the Governor of Madras, the Duke of Buckingham and Chandos.

A large number of boats brought firewood, paddy, and other merchandise from Andhra till the 1960s through the Canal | Photo Credit: The Hindu Archives

Vital link

Running along the coast for about 450 km (250 km in Andhra Pradesh and 200 km in Tamil Nadu), the B’Canal, taken together with the Krishna and Godavari irrigation canal systems, was once a continuous, navigable stretch of about 650 km. Connecting the Marakkanam backwaters in the erstwhile South Arcot (Villupuram) district (115 km south of Chennai), the waterway had been popular as a cheap means of transportation, though the revenue derived from the traffic had never been commensurate with the expenditure involved in keeping it fit for navigation all year round, The Hindu reported on May 3, 1978. In fact, veteran Tamil poet Bharathidasan, in one of his works, mentioned the boat ride he took from Chennai to Mamallapuram along with his friends in 1934. The waterway helped connect Chennai with places such as Kakinada, Rajamahendravaram, Eluru, Vijayawada, Machilipatnam, Ongole, and Nellore.

The B’Canal once had 28 locks, of which 21 were in the northern section of the canal and the rest in the south. Each of the locks had dimensions of 45.5 metres by six metres. “A draught of one metre is available in the northern canal and less in the southern canal,” said this newspaper in 1978. When the erstwhile Madras Presidency was in existence (in 1952-53), about 2.11 lakh tonnes of goods, valued at ₹3.75 crore, were moved on the Canal. Nine years later, 1.47 lakh tonnes of goods were transported along the stretch running through Tamil Nadu. Gradually, passenger traffic along the waterway went down, with other modes of transport gaining popularity.

Poisonous foam from factory effluences mixed with sewage water flowing into the Buckingham Canal near Neelankarai in July 2008 | Photo Credit: M. Karunakaran

Pollution

Considering the importance of the waterway, there was nothing surprising about the preoccupation of the establishment and intelligentsia with the renovation of the B’Canal even 75 years ago. On February 18, 1951, The Hindu, in its editorial, had this to say: “At present, the Canal is a convenient receptacle for the drainage of Madras: with a determined effort at improvement, it can be very much more useful, helping to carry very much larger cargoes than at present, of grains, salt, fish, firewood, chunam shells and charcoal to the City of Madras. Provided its smell disappears, even passengers may use it more and more; even now, from Madras southward, the boats do carry passengers.”

Over these years, a number of studies have been carried out on ways to make the Canal and other watercourses clean and free of pollution, and, if possible, navigable. The issue of bad odour has persisted throughout, even in the 1950s, when Chennai was beginning to expand southwards more than northwards. N. Ranga Reddi, Minister for Public Works, told the Legislative Council on March 19, 1953, that “in regard to the odour nuisance, the sources of pollution have been located and a programme of remedial measures has been fixed by the Superintending Engineer of the Madras Circle [of the Public Works Department] and the Sanitary Engineer.” He added that, apart from “a number of improvements” made in recent years to the Canal, a proposal to increase its width and depth was under consideration by the government.

As the Chennai Municipal Corporation (now called Greater Chennai Corporation) was responsible for the collection and disposal of sewage until the creation of Chennai Metrowater in 1978, it was held responsible for the pollution of the Canal and the Cooum. A high-level committee, constituted by the government in 1960, recommended that, to make the Canal and the Cooum “tidy and clean,” the Corporation be dissuaded from letting sewage into the watercourses, reported The Hindu on March 12, 1960.

Efforts to improve Canal

Even as the State government had plans to deepen the Canal in the 1960s, the banks of the waterway became a convenient site for the growth of slum settlements in the city. People from economically weaker sections, many of whom worked in plumbing, electrical works, and housekeeping, found accommodation along the banks, while the ruling Congress, in the 1950s and 1960s, did little to prevent the areas from being converted into slums. Meanwhile, efforts were on to make at least some stretches of the Canal navigable. In 1981, a comprehensive feasibility study on interlinking canals for navigation between Chennai and Kakinada was mooted with German assistance. The watercourses identified were the Buckingham Canal, Commamur Canal, Eluru Canal, and Kakinada Canal.

Settlements on the banks of the Cooum river | Photo Credit: B. Jothi Ramalingam

As the B’Canal fell into disuse in the 1970s and ‘80s, the State and Central governments drew up a plan to implement the Mass Rapid Transit System (MRTS), using the Canal’s alignment in the central part of Chennai. In no time, elevated structures of the MRTS came up on the banks of the Canal. In November 1995, the first phase of the MRTS — Chennai Beach to Chepauk — was opened to the public. Two years later, the services were extended to Mylapore; in January 2004, to Thiruvanmiyur; over three and a half years later, to Velachery; and in March 2026, to St. Thomas Mount. For about 15 km, up to Thiruvanmiyur, the MRTS structures have come up on the banks of the Buckingham Canal, drastically shrinking the width of the waterway in many places.

When the authorities were considering closing the central segment of the Buckingham Canal — from the Cooum Lock near Sivananda Salai and behind the Madras University campus to the Adyar Lock near Greenways Salai, R.A. Puram — and developing the reclaimed area commercially, Chennai witnessed floods in June 1996, which was unusual for that period. Many parts of central Chennai, including Mylapore, were severely affected. The government dropped the idea of “killing” the central B’ Canal and, instead, decided to make the watercourse functional. What should not be overlooked is that the B’ Canal, if maintained properly, can function as an effective flood carrier during heavy rain.

Desilting programme

Thanks to an intensive desilting programme carried out during the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) regime of 1996-2001, the southern portion of the waterway, a 14-km stretch between Thoraipakkam and Muttukadu, became navigable again. “The canal’s original width of 23 metres (about 75 ft) has been restored and boat services are looked upon as a distinct possibility,” this journalist wrote in The Hindu on June 17, 2000. Days later, the then Minister for Public Works, Duraimurugan, inspected the improved waterway and took this journalist on a boat ride along the stretch.

The inauguration of a 50-metre trash barrier at Buckingham Canal, Vettuvankeni, in January 2026, aimed at reducing plastic leakage into Chennai’s waterways | Photo Credit: V. Umesh Kumar

As there was no follow-up, the Canal had its bad days again. The Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) had even toyed with the idea of making it navigable for about 45 km from Thiruvanmiyur to Kalpakkam, according to a report in this newspaper on September 2, 2014.

Two years later, the proposal was shelved, and the IWAI shifted its office from Uthandi, near Chennai, to Vijayawada in Andhra Pradesh. The only saving grace was that the Union government declared, in April 2016, the 316-km North Buckingham Canal (Peddaganjam-Central Station, Chennai) and the 110-km South Buckingham Canal (Central Station-Marakkanam) as stretches of National Waterway 4.

Having secured the lion’s share of Assembly constituencies that are located along the B’Canal, the ruling TVK has the responsibility to make the watercourse not only a functional flood carrier but also an effective waterway.

Connecting the Marakkanam backwaters in the erstwhile South Arcot (Villupuram) district (115 km south of Chennai), the waterway had been popular as a cheap means of transportation, though the revenue derived from the traffic had never been commensurate with the expenditure involved in keeping it fit for navigation all year round,
The Hindu
reported on May 3, 1978. In fact, veteran Tamil poet Bharathidasan, in one of his works, mentioned the boat ride he took from Chennai to Mamallapuram along with his friends in 1934. The waterway helped connect Chennai with places such as Kakinada, Rajamahendravaram, Eluru, Vijayawada, Machilipatnam, Ongole, and Nellore.
The B’Canal once had 28 locks, of which 21 were in the northern section of the canal and the rest in the south. Each of the locks had dimensions of 45.5 metres by six metres. “A draught of one metre is available in the northern canal and less in the southern canal,” said this newspaper in 1978. When the erstwhile Madras Presidency was in existence (in 1952-53), about 2.11 lakh tonnes of goods, valued at ₹3.75 crore, were moved on the Canal. Nine years later, 1.47 lakh tonnes of goods were transported along the stretch running through Tamil Nadu. Gradually, passenger traffic along the waterway went down, with other modes of transport gaining popularity.
Poisonous foam from factory effluences mixed with sewage water flowing into the Buckingham Canal near Neelankarai in July 2008
                                                            | Photo Credit: 
                                M. Karunakaran
Pollution
Considering the importance of the waterway, there was nothing surprising about the preoccupation of the establishment and intelligentsia with the renovation of the B’Canal even 75 years ago. On February 18, 1951,
The Hindu
, in its editorial, had this to say: “At present, the Canal is a convenient receptacle for the drainage of Madras: with a determined effort at improvement, it can be very much more useful, helping to carry very much larger cargoes than at present, of grains, salt, fish, firewood,
chunam
shells and charcoal to the City of Madras. Provided its smell disappears, even passengers may use it more and more; even now, from Madras southward, the boats do carry passengers.”
Over these years, a number of studies have been carried out on ways to make the Canal and other watercourses clean and free of pollution, and, if possible, navigable. The issue of bad odour has persisted throughout, even in the 1950s, when Chennai was beginning to expand southwards more than northwards. N. Ranga Reddi, Minister for Public Works, told the Legislative Council on March 19, 1953, that “in regard to the odour nuisance, the sources of pollution have been located and a programme of remedial measures has been fixed by the Superintending Engineer of the Madras Circle [of the Public Works Department] and the Sanitary Engineer.” He added that, apart from “a number of improvements” made in recent years to the Canal, a proposal to increase its width and depth was under consideration by the government.
As the Chennai Municipal Corporation (now called Greater Chennai Corporation) was responsible for the collection and disposal of sewage until the creation of Chennai Metrowater in 1978, it was held responsible for the pollution of the Canal and the Cooum. A high-level committee, constituted by the government in 1960, recommended that, to make the Canal and the Cooum “tidy and clean,” the Corporation be dissuaded from letting sewage into the watercourses, reported
The Hindu
on March 12, 1960.
Efforts to improve Canal
Even as the State government had plans to deepen the Canal in the 1960s, the banks of the waterway became a convenient site for the growth of slum settlements in the city. People from economically weaker sections, many of whom worked in plumbing, electrical works, and housekeeping, found accommodation along the banks, while the ruling Congress, in the 1950s and 1960s, did little to prevent the areas from being converted into slums. Meanwhile, efforts were on to make at least some stretches of the Canal navigable. In 1981, a comprehensive feasibility study on interlinking canals for navigation between Chennai and Kakinada was mooted with German assistance. The watercourses identified were the Buckingham Canal, Commamur Canal, Eluru Canal, and Kakinada Canal.
Settlements on the banks of the Cooum river
                                                            | Photo Credit: 
                                B. Jothi Ramalingam
As the B’Canal fell into disuse in the 1970s and ‘80s, the State and Central governments drew up a plan to implement the Mass Rapid Transit System (MRTS), using the Canal’s alignment in the central part of Chennai. In no time, elevated structures of the MRTS came up on the banks of the Canal. In November 1995, the first phase of the MRTS — Chennai Beach to Chepauk — was opened to the public. Two years later, the services were extended to Mylapore; in January 2004, to Thiruvanmiyur; over three and a half years later, to Velachery; and in March 2026, to St. Thomas Mount. For about 15 km, up to Thiruvanmiyur, the MRTS structures have come up on the banks of the Buckingham Canal, drastically shrinking the width of the waterway in many places.
When the authorities were considering closing the central segment of the Buckingham Canal — from the Cooum Lock near Sivananda Salai and behind the Madras University campus to the Adyar Lock near Greenways Salai, R.A. Puram — and developing the reclaimed area commercially, Chennai witnessed floods in June 1996, which was unusual for that period. Many parts of central Chennai, including Mylapore, were severely affected. The government dropped the idea of “killing” the central B’ Canal and, instead, decided to make the watercourse functional. What should not be overlooked is that the B’ Canal, if maintained properly, can function as an effective flood carrier during heavy rain.
Desilting programme
Thanks to an intensive desilting programme carried out during the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK) regime of 1996-2001, the southern portion of the waterway, a 14-km stretch between Thoraipakkam and Muttukadu, became navigable again. “The canal’s original width of 23 metres (about 75 ft) has been restored and boat services are looked upon as a distinct possibility,” this journalist wrote in
The Hindu
on June 17, 2000. Days later, the then Minister for Public Works, Duraimurugan, inspected the improved waterway and took this journalist on a boat ride along the stretch.
The inauguration of a 50-metre trash barrier at Buckingham Canal, Vettuvankeni, in January 2026, aimed at reducing plastic leakage into Chennai’s waterways
                                                            | Photo Credit: 
                                V. Umesh Kumar
As there was no follow-up, the Canal had its bad days again. The Inland Waterways Authority of India (IWAI) had even toyed with the idea of making it navigable for about 45 km from Thiruvanmiyur to Kalpakkam, according to a report in this newspaper on September 2, 2014.
Two years later, the proposal was shelved, and the IWAI shifted its office from Uthandi, near Chennai, to Vijayawada in Andhra Pradesh. The only saving grace was that the Union government declared, in April 2016, the 316-km North Buckingham Canal (Peddaganjam-Central Station, Chennai) and the 110-km South Buckingham Canal (Central Station-Marakkanam) as stretches of National Waterway 4.
Having secured the lion’s share of Assembly constituencies that are located along the B’Canal, the ruling TVK has the responsibility to make the watercourse not only a functional flood carrier but also an effective waterway.

title: More than 9.3 lakh youth received government jobs in Uttar Pradesh in the last nine years, says CM Yogi
author: Mayank Kumar
content_html:
Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath on Tuesday (August 25, 2026) in Lucknow said the State government will provide appointment letters to one lakh youths over the next six months.

Mr. Adityanath added that more than 9.3 lakh youths had been provided government jobs by his government through a transparent and non-discriminatory process since 2017.

“The government has provided government jobs to more than 9.3 lakh youth in a transparent manner without discrimination over the last nine years. In Uttar Pradesh, one lakh jobs were once only an imagination, but we are going to hand over government job appointment letters to one lakh youth within the next six months. The process of declaring results is underway,” said Mr. Adityanath, addressing a function at Indira Gandhi Pratishthan.

In the function, he handed over appointment letters to 3,446 newly selected Technical Assistants (Group-C) and 126 Mandi Secretaries in the Agriculture Department under Mission Rozgar through the Uttar Pradesh Subordinate Services Selection Commission (UPSSSC). 

Mr. Adityanath urged newly selected candidates that since the government has provided transparent appointments, they should also use this opportunity for the benefit of the State, future generations, and the country. Honest discharge of duty is the theory of “Nation First.”

The Chief Minister further added, “our commissions and boards are effectively ensuring that appointment letters are issued to deserving candidates based on merit through a transparent recruitment process, free from discrimination and in accordance with reservation policies. This is praiseworthy. The selection of the most qualified candidates allows the entire state to harness their energy.”

The Chief Minister told officials of the recruitment commissions and boards, “there is no government interference in your operations. If we have granted you autonomy, then it is imperative to deliver results promptly. The declaration of results should not exceed six months after a requisition is received. Advertisements should be issued within one month, followed by examinations conducted within the subsequent two months. Streamline the process to ensure that the youth can channel their energy effectively. When we advance with the vigor of youth, positive outcomes will ensue.”

Hailing the transparent recruitment over the last nine years as an achievement of the double-engine government of the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the CM accused the previous Samajwadi Party (SP) government of neglecting youths.

“Before 2017, as soon as advertisements were issued, the chacha-bhatija (uncle-nephew) duo and the Mahabharat clan would set out for collections. Youth kept wandering, but results never came. Ultimately, the Hon’ble Court had to stay the process. The time and age of youth were wasted,” he said.

“Young people who failed to get jobs were considered unworthy, but the fault was not of the youth. The fault lay with politicians sitting in the government machinery and dishonest people sitting in commissions and boards. Our government had said that we would break the backbone of the copying mafia and also bring their patrons to the ground. We got mafia properties confiscated and recovered money from them,” the CM added..

Mr. Adityanath said that after becoming Chief Minister in 2017, he directed officials of the Board of Secondary Education to conduct examinations and declare results within one month.

“When the response was negative, I told them, ‘Leave your chairs; I will get it done within a month.’ Today, examinations for 56 lakh candidates of the U.P. Board are completed within 14 days, and results are declared within the next 14 days. Earlier, examinations that started in February continued until the scorching heat of June. Now, examinations are conducted without copying, and results are declared on time. Universities have also been directed to bring reforms. Educational institutions should prepare themselves for students’ skilling, careers, and employment,” he added.

title: Pune tribal students’ protest enters 13th day as talks with Tribal Minister yield no breakthrough, say students
author: Yohaan Varghese
content_html:
The students’ protest at a government tribal boys’ hostel in Pune continued for the 13th day on Tuesday (August 25, 2026), a day after ten students met Tribal Minister Dr. Ashok Ramaji Uike at Mantralaya in Mumbai but failed to secure assurances on their demands.

Vijay Waghmare, a Secretary in the Tribal Department, said that the Ministry has issued a stay order on the major demand of the students, that is, regarding the Government Resolution (GR) issued on August 14, 2026. “The government has met the major demand of the students regarding the Hostel Admissions GR. We have continued to interact with them and responded positively to their other demands. However, it will take time for putting them into action,” he said.

According to Balakrishna Gawari, a member of the Students Federation of India (SFI), the discussions ended without any significant progress or agreement on their demands, and they were asked to continue their protests. “They told us that they could not give us a definite written agreement to their demands, and that we could continue the protests if we wanted to,” he said.

Mr. Gawari also said that the students sought action over an alleged 12,500 government posts reserved for Scheduled Tribes that had been occupied by non-tribal candidates using fake caste certificates. “Those posts should be made vacant and should be filled with deserving people who belong to the Scheduled Tribe, and action should be taken against fake adivasis,” Mr. Gawari said.

Sharad Thokal, 26; Vijay Bhandble, 25; Rahul Dhanwe, 26; and Rajaram Padvi, 20, are continuing their hunger strike at the Adivasi Government Boys Hostel near the Hadapsar-Manjari border. Shweta Girnak, 26; Nikita Mechkar, 22 were admitted to the hospital on Monday evening due to poor health.

Some important demands the tribal students are seeking are that allowances and other financial provisions be linked to the Consumer Price Index so that they increase annually in line with inflation. increased protection for students staying in tribal hostels and ashram schools, and an insurance cover of ₹10 crore for every tribal student. This follows the recent deaths of three tribal students in a snakebite incident in Gadchiroli. The students have also sought compensation of ₹1 crore each for the families.

Other key demands include a safe and well-equipped central hostel building for female students in Pune and the immediate filling of vacant posts in hostels and ashram schools, including posts for peons, security guards, and sanitation workers, either permanently or on a contractual basis until regular recruitment is completed.

title: Suvendu vows to keep Mamata off the streets, TMC chairperson says not taking political sanyas
author: Shiv Sahay Singh
content_html:
Referring to former Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee interacting with her supporters through social media, West Bengal Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari on Monday (August 24, 2026) suggested that his predecessor remains active on Facebook and said that he will ensure that she does not hit the streets.

“Remain active on facebook. You will not have to go out on the streets anymore. I will also make arrangements so that you cannot go out on the streets,” the Chief Minister said, while addressing a press conference at the State Secretariat.

Ms. Banerjee, who only a few hours ago reiterated that she will not be pushed into a political sanyas, described the remark as a threat.

“A NEW LOW in Indian politics! @SuvenduWB, while seated in a government office, has brazenly THREATENED me, publicly declaring that he will ensure I cannot even leave my home. I call upon the Hon’ble President of India, the Hon’ble Chief Justice of India, and the people of India: Is this the India envisioned by our Constitution?” the Trinamool Congress chairperson wrote on X in a late evening post. A number of leaders of the Trinamool Congress joined Ms. Banerjee in taking on the Chief Minister.

After the defeat in the West Bengal Assembly polls 2026, Ms. Banerjee, who made her political mark as a ‘street-fighter ’, has not hit the streets often. On a few occasions she tried to do so the response has been tepid.

Mr. Adhikari cited the two instances of Baruipur, where a minor was raped and killed, and Halisahar, where a Trinamool supporter was killed in police custody and said that she failed at both the occasions.

However, the remark to keep the Trinamool Congress chairperson confined to social media has larger ramifications. Despite her party facing the biggest existential crisis – with majority of MPs and MLAs switching sides and warming up to the BJP, Mamata Banerjee remains the only leader to take on the might of the BJP which has 207 MLAs in a 294 member house.

Over the past few years, the politics in West Bengal has been hinged on a contest between an ageing leader who wants to pass over the baton to her nephew and one of her closest aides turned rival. Suvendu Adhikari has defeated Mamata Banerjee directly in an electoral contest on two occasions — in Nandigram in the 2021 Assembly polls by a margin of 1956 votes and in 2026 at Bhabanipur by a margin of 15,065 votes. The 2026 Assembly polls might not be the end of political rivalry, and people of West Bengal may continue to see the two political personalities taking on each other.

There is an enthusiasm among the BJP leadership after coming to power, but the Suvendu Adhikari government is caught in the same policy trap of giving cash doles which had been a hallmark of the Trinamool Congress regime. 

With women protesting the denial of cash incentives under Annapurna Bhandar scheme as promised by the BJP during the election campaign, Mamata Banerjee sees it as an opportunity to revive both her credibility and her party.

There is also unease among the leaders who left Mamata Banerjee to warm up to the BJP, particularly those who are from the minority community, and that can be a silver lining for the Trinamool Congress chairperson. For Suvendu Adhikari, the challenge is how long can they keep the former Chief Minister confined to her residence and social media.
